alternativeNames.name: Ilion
alternativeNames.note: Greek name used for the later city and in ancient tradition

chronology.label: Bronze Age fortified settlements
chronology.note: The conventional Troy I–VII sequence groups a succession of fortified Bronze Age settlements on Hisarlık. The nine-city framework is an archaeological periodisation, not evidence for nine unrelated cities.

chronology.label: Troy I–V
chronology.note: Early Bronze Age and early Middle Bronze Age settlement phases include Troy II, the period associated with Schliemann's famous treasure finds and with substantial megaron architecture.

chronology.label: Troy VI
chronology.note: A monumental Late Bronze Age citadel with massive stone fortifications and evidence for a substantial lower settlement. Its final destruction is widely associated with earthquake damage rather than a securely identified war event.

chronology.label: Troy VIIa
chronology.note: The settlement reused the Troy VI fortifications in a more densely occupied citadel and ended in a destructive episode. Its chronology falls within the broad historical horizon in which later Greek traditions placed a Trojan conflict, but archaeology does not identify a specific Homeric war.

chronology.label: Troy VIIb
chronology.note: Post-Bronze Age occupation continued through several subphases as regional political systems changed after the collapse of the Late Bronze Age world.

chronology.label: Greek and Hellenistic Ilion
chronology.note: The mound and lower city became the Greek city of Ilion. Sanctuaries and later Hellenistic monumental building reused a landscape already charged with Trojan memory.

chronology.label: Roman Ilium
chronology.note: Roman rebuilding produced public monuments including the odeion and bouleuterion, while the city's claimed connection to Trojan ancestry remained politically and culturally productive.

historicalContext.text: Troy occupies Hisarlık near the southern entrance to the Dardanelles, a position linking inland Anatolia with the Aegean, Balkans and Black Sea routes. The site preserves a long sequence of fortified Bronze Age settlements beneath and alongside the later Greek and Roman city of Ilion. UNESCO describes Troy as a key archaeological record for contacts between Anatolian and Mediterranean worlds, while current research continues to refine the scale, chronology and regional role of the settlement.

archaeologicalSignificance.text: Troy is methodologically important because its archaeological sequence, literary afterlife and excavation history cannot be separated cleanly. The site shaped Bronze Age chronology, generated long-running debates about the relationship between Hisarlık, Hittite Wilusa and Greek epic, and became an early public symbol of archaeology itself. Its significance therefore lies not in proving a single legendary event, but in the interaction between settlement evidence, historical texts, later memory and changing archaeological practice.

excavationHistory.text: Frank Calvert began excavating at Hisarlık in 1863 before Heinrich Schliemann's campaigns from 1870. Wilhelm Dörpfeld later revised Schliemann's identification of Troy II as the Homeric city by exposing the monumental Troy VI fortifications. Carl Blegen's University of Cincinnati excavations from 1932 to 1938 subdivided the mound into dozens of strata within nine major settlement horizons. The Tübingen–Cincinnati project resumed large-scale research from 1988, combining Bronze Age and post-Bronze Age investigation. Since 2015, excavations have been directed by Rüstem Aslan of Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University; the 2024 season included work in the agora and around the Troy VI palace area, and 2025 fieldwork produced a gold ring-brooch and rare jade object from an Early Bronze Age context around 2500 BCE.

narrativeSections.label: Stratigraphy
narrativeSections.title: The famous “nine cities” are an analytical framework, not nine clean beginnings.
paragraphs: Blegen's excavations distinguished roughly forty-six strata and grouped them into nine major horizons. That system made Troy a reference point for Aegean and Anatolian chronology, but the numbered cities can easily create a false image of repeated abandonment and replacement.

In practice, rebuilding, reuse and continuity cross many of the boundaries. Troy VI and early Troy VII, for example, share fortifications and settlement history even though excavation terminology gives them different numbers.

narrativeSections.label: Bronze Age city
narrativeSections.title: The citadel is only part of Late Bronze Age Troy.
paragraphs: The monumental sloping walls of Troy VI dominate the visitor experience, but research south of the mound has demonstrated that settlement extended well beyond the fortified citadel. UNESCO describes a Late Bronze Age lower city of about thirty hectares, while survey research cautions that its building density and internal organisation cannot yet be reconstructed with equal confidence everywhere.

This distinction matters. Troy was not simply a small fortress on a hill; neither does the archaeological evidence justify turning every square metre within the defensive system into densely built urban fabric.

narrativeSections.label: Text and archaeology
narrativeSections.title: Homer is reception history, not an excavation diary.
paragraphs: Late Bronze Age Troy occupies the only chronological horizon that could plausibly underlie much later Greek traditions of a Trojan conflict. Hittite texts referring to Wilusa and Ahhiyawa provide an independent political context for western Anatolia, and many scholars consider an identification of Wilusa with Troy plausible.

None of this converts the Iliad into a literal historical report. The poem took shape centuries after the Late Bronze Age, and the surviving archaeological record cannot identify Achilles, Priam, a ten-year siege or a single event matching the epic narrative.

narrativeSections.label: Greek and Roman Ilion
narrativeSections.title: Later cities built with the authority of an already ancient past.
paragraphs: Greek and Roman Ilion developed on and around the Bronze Age mound rather than beside an abandoned ruin. Sanctuaries, the Temple of Athena, the agora, odeion and bouleuterion inserted new civic architecture into a landscape whose Trojan associations had become culturally valuable.

Under Hellenistic and Roman rule, Troy's legendary ancestry became part of political memory. Archaeology therefore records not only survival after the Bronze Age, but active reuse of the past as a civic resource.

narrativeSections.label: History of archaeology
narrativeSections.title: Troy preserves the consequences of archaeology itself.
paragraphs: Schliemann's drive to reach what he believed was Homeric Troy cut through and removed substantial later deposits. Dörpfeld and Blegen subsequently revised the site's chronology through more systematic architectural and stratigraphic work, while later projects added geophysics, archaeometry, digital documentation and lower-city survey.

The famous trench is therefore not merely damage to hide. It is evidence for how archaeological questions, techniques and ethical standards changed—and for how interpretation can be permanently constrained by earlier excavation decisions.

narrativeSections.label: Current research
narrativeSections.title: A 2025 find shifts attention back toward Troy's Early Bronze Age networks.
paragraphs: In 2025, the Turkish excavation project announced a gold ring-brooch from a context dated around 2500 BCE together with a bronze pin and a rare jade object. The finds were assigned to Troy's Early Bronze Age sequence and are planned for display in the Troy Museum.

Their value for the archive is not that they produce another treasure story. They reopen questions of status, craft, material circulation and long-distance connection in a phase of Troy that predates the Late Bronze Age city by more than a millennium.

editorialNotes: The record distinguishes archaeological Troy from later Trojan War traditions. Possible connections with Hittite Wilusa are presented as a scholarly hypothesis, not as proof that the Iliad records a specific historical siege. The conventional Troy I–IX sequence is treated as archaeological periodisation rather than a literal succession of nine unrelated cities.
